To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we generated and characterized three monoclonal antibodies (Mbv2A10, Mav3H11, and Mar2D10) that recognize proteins of the Mycobacteriaceae family.
three new mAbs against M. bovis BCG Mexico, M. arubense and M. avim were developed and characterized.

the Mbv2A, Mav3H and Mar2D mAbs are specific for M. bovis BCG, M. avium and M. arupense, respectively; these mAbs recognize a number of proteins that have important roles in metabolic processes; and these mAbs have cross‐reactivity against a number of mycobacteria, including the M. tuberculosis complex, M. kansasii, M. marinum and M. avium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the production and characterization of mAb clones with the highest recognition of M. bovism, M. avian and M. arupe, and with the identification of proteins recognized by mAbs.
the identification of proteins recognized by these mAbs and their potential cross‐reactivity, which is of great interest in the study of tuberculosis, NTM, and the development of new vaccines.
the production of mAb that can potentially be used in the detection of mycobacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these mAb clones could be useful for the diagnosis and characterization of mycobacteria.
the mAbs generated against mycobacteria could be used for diagnosis, vaccine development, and as a tool for understanding the pathogenesis of these pathogens.
the Mbv 2a10 and Mav 3h1 monoclonal antibodies have the potential to be useful for the diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of mycobacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Mbv2A, Mav3H, and Mar2D mAbs could be useful tools in the diagnosis of mycobacterial diseases and for studying the immunological response to mycobacteria in humans.

the selected clones have cross‐reactivity against M. bovistuberculosis and M. avim and M. aupense strains, which may be used in further studies to identify proteins that could be potential candidates for vaccine and diagnostic purposes.
the selected mAb clones have a potential cross‐reactivity against mycobacteria and can be used as a tool for mycobacterial diagnosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
these mAbs are potential tools for diagnostic purposes and could be used as reagents for the development of vaccines against mycobacteria.
